0.1.explanation: A computer follows instructions by moving data between a processor, working memory, storage, and input/output devices. A CPU runs general instructions; a GPU repeats many numerical operations at once.
0.1.why: Hardware limits explain why a model fits in RAM but fails in GPU memory.
0.1.application: Choosing a machine for a local inference service.
0.1.assignment: Inspect your machine's CPU cores, RAM, disk and GPU. Draw the path of a Python program from disk to execution and record a real memory measurement.

0.2.explanation: An operating system shares hardware between running programs. Its kernel schedules work, manages memory, and controls device access; applications normally run with fewer privileges in user space.
0.2.why: Processes, resource limits and scheduling affect API reliability.
0.2.application: Diagnosing a backend that consumes too much memory.
0.2.assignment: Run two Python processes, inspect their process IDs and memory, then stop one gracefully. Reproduce a small race condition and fix it with a lock.

0.3.explanation: A network lets machines exchange messages. DNS finds an address, TCP provides an ordered byte stream, TLS protects transport, and HTTP defines the request and response used by most web APIs.
0.3.why: An AI provider call crosses a network that can be slow or fail.
0.3.application: Tracing a request from a browser to an inference API.
0.3.assignment: Use browser developer tools and curl to inspect a request, its headers, TLS connection and response status. Compare a successful request with a missing route.

0.4.explanation: A terminal is a text interface to a shell. The shell starts programs and connects files, processes and environment settings, making repeatable development and server work possible.
0.4.why: Production debugging often happens without a graphical desktop.
0.4.application: Starting a Python service on a Linux server.
0.4.assignment: Create a Linux practice directory, a virtual environment and a script. Set a temporary environment variable, redirect logs and inspect the running process.

0.5.explanation: Git records snapshots of a project's history. Branches let you change code independently; GitHub hosts repositories and adds review through pull requests.
0.5.why: Version history lets you review, collaborate and recover safely.
0.5.application: Reviewing a model-serving change before release.
0.5.assignment: Create a repository, ignore generated files, make two branches, resolve a deliberate merge conflict, and open a pull request with a useful README.

1.1.explanation: Python is a general-purpose language used to describe computations using values, control flow and collections. Its interpreter executes your code while the standard library supplies reusable tools.
1.1.why: You need fluent programming before model libraries become useful.
1.1.application: Validating and transforming a batch of prediction requests.
1.1.assignment: Build a command-line marks calculator that validates input, uses a dictionary of students and prints a formatted summary. Test empty and invalid input.

1.2.explanation: Functions give a named operation a clear input and output. Modules and packages group these operations so a program can grow without becoming one tangled script.
1.2.why: Small explicit interfaces make AI pipelines easier to test and change.
1.2.application: Separating data loading, preprocessing and prediction.
1.2.assignment: Split the marks calculator into modules. Write pure functions for validation and aggregation, demonstrate positional and keyword arguments, and test edge cases.

1.3.explanation: Object-oriented programming combines state and behavior in objects. Classes define their structure; composition assembles behavior from smaller objects, and polymorphism allows interchangeable implementations.
1.3.why: A common interface keeps provider-specific code out of business logic.
1.3.application: Implementing two model providers behind one interface.
1.3.assignment: Create Student and StudentRepository classes. Add a file-backed repository, replace it with an in-memory version in tests, and explain why composition helps.

1.4.explanation: Python's advanced tools control errors, iteration, resource lifetimes and asynchronous work. Generators produce values lazily; async I/O lets a program wait for external work without blocking all other tasks.
1.4.why: Data and API code must handle large inputs and partial failure.
1.4.application: Streaming records into a preprocessing pipeline.
1.4.assignment: Build a typed JSON-to-CSV converter with a generator, a context manager, structured logs and custom exceptions. Add an async example with bounded concurrency.

1.5.explanation: Professional Python development makes behavior predictable through consistent formatting, types, tests and documentation. Profiling measures actual bottlenecks before you optimize.
1.5.why: Readable, checked code is easier to maintain than a clever untested script.
1.5.application: Preparing a small Python package for a team.
1.5.assignment: Add a formatter, linter, type checker and pytest suite to your package. Use fixtures and one dependency mock, then profile a real slow path.

1.6-javascript.explanation: JavaScript runs interactive web applications; TypeScript adds static checks around its values and interfaces. Promises model asynchronous work such as a network request.
1.6-javascript.why: An AI application needs a usable, reliable interface around its backend.
1.6-javascript.application: Building a typed frontend for a prediction API.
1.6-javascript.assignment: Build a small TypeScript client with a typed request and response, a loading state and a visible error state. Validate network input at runtime as well.

1.6-sql.explanation: SQL describes queries and changes to relational tables. Keys and constraints protect relationships, while joins combine related records without copying them everywhere.
1.6-sql.why: Most applications need durable, queryable user and request data.
1.6-sql.application: Reporting token usage per account in PostgreSQL.
1.6-sql.assignment: Create students and results tables. Write filtered, joined and grouped queries; add constraints, an index and a transaction. Use parameters for user input.

1.6-bash.explanation: Bash is a command shell and scripting language for connecting programs, files and environment settings. Exit codes let scripts detect failed steps.
1.6-bash.why: Repeatable automation reduces mistakes during setup and deployment.
1.6-bash.application: Automating a local test and packaging workflow.
1.6-bash.assignment: Write a script that checks its inputs, runs tests, writes a timestamped log and exits on failure. Practice only in a temporary directory.

2.1.explanation: Basic mathematics describes quantities and relationships. Algebra turns an unknown value into a solvable equation; functions map inputs to outputs, and graphs reveal their behavior.
2.1.why: Ratios, logarithms and functions appear in costs, loss curves and scaling.
2.1.application: Calculating growth in data size and request cost.
2.1.assignment: Plot a linear and a quadratic function in Python. Solve sample equations and calculate percentage error and a token budget by hand, then verify with code.

2.2.explanation: Discrete mathematics studies countable objects and logical statements. Sets describe membership, logic expresses rules, and graphs model relationships between entities.
2.2.why: Algorithms and access-control rules depend on precise reasoning.
2.2.application: Representing relationships in a knowledge system.
2.2.assignment: Build truth tables for a small access policy, count possible combinations, and model a course prerequisite graph. Explain a proof by induction.

2.3.explanation: Statistics summarizes observations and reasons about a population from a sample. Variation, sampling and uncertainty matter as much as a single average.
2.3.why: A model score without uncertainty can hide poor real-world performance.
2.3.application: Comparing error rates across user groups.
2.3.assignment: Analyze a small public dataset. Report center, spread, missingness and a confidence interval; explain selection bias and why correlation does not prove causation.

2.4.explanation: Probability models uncertain outcomes. Conditional probability updates a probability when evidence is known; Bayes' theorem relates that update to prior beliefs and likelihoods.
2.4.why: Prediction, classification and experimentation require reasoning about uncertainty.
2.4.assignment: Simulate repeated coin flips, calculate a conditional probability and solve a Bayes example using invented classroom numbers.

2.5.explanation: Linear algebra represents numerical data as vectors and matrices. Matrix multiplication combines transformations; a dot product measures how two vectors align.
2.5.why: Embeddings, attention and neural layers are vector and matrix operations.
2.5.assignment: Implement vector dot product and matrix multiplication by hand for tiny arrays. Verify with NumPy and draw a two-dimensional linear transformation.

2.6.explanation: Calculus describes how outputs change as inputs change. A derivative measures local change; gradients collect partial derivatives and guide optimization toward lower loss.
2.6.why: Backpropagation is an efficient application of the chain rule.
2.6.application: Training a simple linear regression model.
2.6.assignment: Differentiate a squared-error function, compare the result with finite differences, and implement gradient descent with several learning rates.

2.7.explanation: Information theory quantifies uncertainty and the difference between probability distributions. Entropy measures uncertainty; cross-entropy scores predictions against observed outcomes.
2.7.why: Classification and language-model losses use these quantities.
2.7.application: Explaining why a confident wrong prediction has a high loss.
2.7.assignment: Compute entropy for a fair and biased coin. Calculate cross-entropy and KL divergence for tiny distributions, carefully handling zero probabilities.

2.8.explanation: Data structures organize values and algorithms describe the steps used to process them. Complexity estimates how time or memory grows with input size.
2.8.why: Choosing a hash map or queue can matter more than choosing a framework.
2.8.application: Scheduling requests and searching a document graph.
2.8.assignment: Implement binary search, a queue and BFS. Solve a small set of problems, record edge cases and derive time and space complexity for each solution.

3.1.explanation: Software engineering turns requirements into maintainable, tested programs. Clear boundaries separate responsibilities so changes stay local and behavior can be reviewed.
3.1.why: A working prototype becomes fragile when every feature depends on everything else.
3.1.application: Designing a service that supports multiple model providers.
3.1.assignment: Write functional and quality requirements, split an application into modules, review a change, refactor duplicated behavior and write an architecture decision.

3.2.explanation: PostgreSQL stores related data in tables and provides transactions, constraints and a query planner. Indexes speed selected reads at a cost to writes and storage.
3.2.why: AI products still need correct user, document and usage records.
3.2.application: Persisting request history with tenant isolation.
3.2.assignment: Design a schema for users, documents and requests. Add keys and constraints, inspect EXPLAIN output, run a transaction and test backup restoration.

3.3.explanation: NoSQL is a family of database approaches including documents, key-value records, wide columns and graphs. Each makes different choices about queries, relationships and scaling.
3.3.why: Data shape and access patterns should drive storage decisions.
3.3.application: Comparing MongoDB documents with relational tables.
3.3.assignment: Model the same document metadata in PostgreSQL and MongoDB. List the queries each model supports well and document consistency and indexing trade-offs.

3.4.explanation: Data engineering moves data from sources into useful, trustworthy forms. Pipelines ingest, validate, transform and store data while recording its origin and failures.
3.4.why: A model cannot compensate for a silently broken data pipeline.
3.4.assignment: Build a CSV-to-Parquet pipeline with schema validation, duplicate handling, a quarantine file and rerunnable steps. Record source, version and row counts.

3.5.explanation: AI storage combines ordinary records with document content and numerical embeddings. Metadata connects vectors back to their source and access permissions.
3.5.why: Retrieval must return relevant content that the requesting user may access.
3.5.application: Designing storage for a document assistant.
3.5.assignment: Design users, documents, chunks and embedding tables. Include tenant filters, source versions and deletion behavior; explain the hybrid retrieval query.

4.1.explanation: Data science explores data to answer questions. NumPy computes over arrays, Pandas organizes labeled tables, and charts help reveal distributions and mistakes.
4.1.why: Exploration exposes leakage, missing data and unsuitable assumptions early.
4.1.application: Understanding a dataset before training a predictor.
4.1.assignment: Create a reproducible notebook that profiles a public dataset, cleans it without hiding issues, and explains three useful charts in plain English.

4.2.explanation: Machine learning fits a model to examples rather than specifying every rule. Training chooses parameters; inference uses the resulting model on new input.
4.2.why: A useful model must generalize beyond its training examples.
4.2.application: Predicting an outcome from structured features.
4.2.assignment: Create train, validation and test splits before preprocessing. Train a simple baseline and demonstrate how accidental data leakage inflates a score.

4.3.explanation: Supervised learning uses labeled examples to learn a mapping from features to a target. Linear methods, trees and ensembles make different assumptions about that mapping.
4.3.why: A small baseline can beat a complex model on cost and reliability.
4.3.application: Selecting a model for tabular prediction.
4.3.assignment: Compare a linear model, decision tree and random forest using the same splits and metric. Explain errors, training cost and why one model fits the task.

4.4.explanation: Unsupervised learning looks for structure without target labels. Clustering groups similar observations; dimensionality reduction creates a smaller representation.
4.4.why: It supports exploration and anomaly discovery when labels are unavailable.
4.4.assignment: Scale a small dataset, compare K-Means and DBSCAN, visualize PCA projections and explain why cluster labels are not automatically meaningful categories.

4.5.explanation: Evaluation connects predictions to the real cost of mistakes. Classification metrics describe different errors; regression metrics describe numerical distance from targets.
4.5.why: High accuracy can hide a model that ignores a rare important class.
4.5.application: Choosing a threshold for a spam detector.
4.5.assignment: Compute a confusion matrix and precision, recall and F1 by hand. Compare thresholds, use cross-validation and report one subgroup failure.

4.6.explanation: Model improvement combines preprocessing, feature design and controlled hyperparameter experiments. A pipeline keeps transformations consistent between training and inference.
4.6.why: Uncontrolled experiments make gains difficult to trust or reproduce.
4.6.application: Improving and packaging a baseline predictor.
4.6.assignment: Build a scikit-learn Pipeline, compare a small search space with cross-validation, record seeds and parameters, and save the complete inference pipeline.

5.1.explanation: Deep learning uses layered numerical transformations whose parameters are learned from data. Forward passes produce predictions; backpropagation computes gradients for optimization.
5.1.why: Understanding the training loop helps explain instability and overfitting.
5.1.application: Training a small classifier from feature vectors.
5.1.assignment: Implement a tiny network, inspect gradients and plot training versus validation loss. Compare learning rates and one regularization method.

5.2.explanation: PyTorch represents data as tensors and records operations for automatic differentiation. Modules define networks, while optimizers update learnable parameters.
5.2.why: It makes model mechanics explicit and debuggable.
5.2.application: Writing a custom training and evaluation loop.
5.2.assignment: Train a small PyTorch classifier with batches, zero_grad, backward and optimizer.step. Save and reload weights and verify predictions in evaluation mode.

5.3.explanation: Neural architectures encode assumptions about data. CNNs use local spatial patterns, recurrent networks process sequences, and attention combines information across positions.
5.3.why: Architecture choices influence accuracy, memory and computation.
5.3.application: Choosing a model for images versus text.
5.3.assignment: Compare a small feedforward model with a CNN on images. Trace tensor shapes and explain where recurrent models and transformers would be appropriate.

5.4.explanation: A GPU runs many numerical operations in parallel but has limited device memory. Precision, batch size and data movement affect both speed and stability.
5.4.why: A training job can run out of memory long before a GPU is fully utilized.
5.4.assignment: Estimate parameter, gradient and optimizer memory for a tiny model. Measure batch throughput and memory; compare CPU with an available GPU without requiring paid hardware.

6.1.explanation: Natural language processing turns text into representations that programs can analyze. Tokenization, normalization and embeddings prepare input for classification and retrieval.
6.1.why: Text preprocessing choices can remove useful meaning or introduce bias.
6.1.assignment: Compare TF-IDF with a small embedding representation on sample documents. Inspect tokenization, named entities and errors on unusual text.

6.2.explanation: A language model assigns probabilities to text sequences, often by predicting the next token. Training learns parameters; inference produces probabilities from fixed parameters.
6.2.why: This explains both fluent generation and its factual limitations.
6.2.assignment: Tokenize several sentences, inspect IDs and lengths, and manually trace a toy next-token distribution. Distinguish pretraining, fine-tuning and inference.

6.3.explanation: A transformer mixes information between token positions using attention. Queries compare with keys to produce weights over values; residual paths and normalization stabilize stacked layers.
6.3.why: Attention and tensor shapes explain context handling and compute cost.
6.3.application: Understanding the architecture behind a decoder language model.
6.3.assignment: Implement scaled dot-product attention on tiny matrices. Add a causal mask, check shapes and explain why future tokens must be hidden during training.

6.4.explanation: LLM generation repeatedly processes a context, computes next-token probabilities and selects a token. Sampling changes the output distribution; caching avoids recomputing prior key/value states.
6.4.why: Decoding and context length affect quality, latency and memory.
6.4.application: Tuning an inference service's generation settings.
6.4.assignment: Compare greedy, top-k and top-p decoding on a toy distribution. Record token count, time to first token and generation speed for a small available model.

6.5.explanation: Adaptation changes an existing model for a narrower task. Fine-tuning updates parameters, LoRA trains small low-rank updates, and preference methods optimize against comparison data.
6.5.why: Adaptation is useful only when evaluation supports its cost and risks.
6.5.application: Planning a task-specific model adaptation experiment.
6.5.assignment: Prepare a small licensed instruction dataset, separate evaluation examples and compare prompting with a lightweight adaptation plan. Document overfitting and license risks.

6.6.explanation: Hugging Face hosts models, datasets and libraries that make existing models easier to load and evaluate. Model cards explain intended use, limits and licenses.
6.6.why: Using a model safely requires more than copying its identifier.
6.6.application: Selecting and loading a suitable open model.
6.6.assignment: Inspect a model card and license, pin a revision, load its tokenizer and run a small CPU-compatible example. Record configuration and evaluation results.

7.1.explanation: An API is a contract between programs. HTTP APIs use routes, methods, schemas and status codes to make requests and responses predictable.
7.1.why: Reliable contracts keep clients independent of backend internals.
7.1.assignment: Specify a prediction endpoint with validation, pagination and errors. Document authentication, timeout and retry behavior using an OpenAPI schema.

7.2.explanation: FastAPI is a Python web framework that uses type annotations and Pydantic validation to define HTTP endpoints. Async endpoints help with waiting on I/O, not CPU-heavy computation.
7.2.why: It provides a practical bridge between Python models and clients.
7.2.assignment: Build a validated prediction endpoint, inject a model service, add consistent errors and test successful and invalid requests with a test client.

7.3.explanation: Backend architecture separates transport, application rules and persistence. A route translates HTTP, a service performs a use case and a repository handles storage.
7.3.why: Changing a provider or database should not require rewriting every endpoint.
7.3.assignment: Separate an API into routes, services and repositories. Replace one dependency in tests and prove that validation and business rules stay consistent.

7.4.explanation: A provider adapter converts your application's common request format into a provider-specific API call. It normalizes responses, streaming events and failures.
7.4.why: Provider differences should be explicit rather than scattered throughout the app.
7.4.application: Connecting two providers behind a stable interface.
7.4.assignment: Define an adapter protocol and implement two mocked providers. Validate structured responses, normalize errors, apply timeouts and keep credentials server-side.

7.5.explanation: LLM tokens are pieces of text used for processing and billing. They are unrelated to authentication tokens and API keys. Input, output and cached token rates may differ.
7.5.why: Budgets and quotas require measured usage and current provider pricing.
7.5.application: Estimating and enforcing a request budget.
7.5.assignment: Build a token-cost calculator using configurable rates, separate input and output usage, check context limits and enforce an account budget with a reserve.

7.6.explanation: AI backend reliability anticipates slow providers, malformed responses and interrupted streams. Bounded retries, circuit breakers and idempotency prevent failures from multiplying.
7.6.why: A fallback without limits can increase both outages and cost.
7.6.assignment: Simulate timeout, rate-limit and malformed-response failures. Add jittered backoff, a retry budget, cancellation and a circuit breaker; verify usage is not counted twice.

8.1.explanation: Embeddings represent items as numerical vectors so similarity can be computed. The embedding model defines the representation; distance alone does not guarantee semantic correctness.
8.1.why: Retrieval quality depends on representation, indexing and evaluation.
8.1.assignment: Embed a small corpus with one model, compare cosine and dot-product rankings and test queries with known relevant results. Keep model and dimensions consistent.

8.2.explanation: A vector database stores embeddings and searches nearby vectors, often using approximate indexes. Metadata filtering restricts candidate records by attributes or permissions.
8.2.why: The database must meet recall, latency and operational requirements.
8.2.application: Storing document chunks in PostgreSQL with pgvector.
8.2.assignment: Start with pgvector, create vectors and metadata, compare exact and indexed search, and measure recall and latency. Explore alternatives only if needed.

8.3.explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation finds relevant external content and includes it in a model's context. It changes supplied information without retraining model weights.
8.3.why: Sources can improve grounding but retrieval and generation can still fail.
8.3.assignment: Parse a small document set, chunk it, retrieve context and generate answers with source references. Include unanswerable questions and permission-filtered documents.

8.4.explanation: Advanced retrieval improves a measured baseline using methods such as hybrid search, query rewriting and reranking. Each additional stage adds latency and failure modes.
8.4.why: Sophisticated retrieval should earn its complexity through evaluation.
8.4.application: Improving document recall for ambiguous queries.
8.4.assignment: Build a labeled query set, compare keyword and vector retrieval, add a reranker and measure recall, faithfulness, latency and citation correctness.

8.5.explanation: A knowledge graph stores entities as nodes and relationships as edges. Traversal follows these connections to answer relationship-oriented questions.
8.5.why: Explicit relationships can support multi-hop explanations.
8.5.application: Connecting papers, authors and research topics.
8.5.assignment: Build a small graph with provenance on every relation. Write traversal queries, resolve duplicate entities and compare results with a flat document index.

8.6.explanation: Graph RAG uses graph relationships during retrieval before constructing a model's context. It can help connected questions but adds extraction, storage and maintenance cost.
8.6.why: It is a situational extension rather than a universal replacement for vector RAG.
8.6.assignment: Build a small provenance-aware graph and compare graph, vector and hybrid retrieval on relationship questions. Report extraction errors and operational cost.

8.7.explanation: An agent uses a model to choose actions within a loop of observation, tool execution and state updates. A workflow can keep more of that sequence deterministic.
8.7.why: Tool access turns model mistakes into real actions unless permissions are bounded.
8.7.application: Running a research workflow with approved tools.
8.7.assignment: Build a bounded agent loop using mocked tools, explicit state, time and cost budgets, an allowlist and human approval before a sensitive operation.

8.8.explanation: Frameworks provide reusable orchestration, while protocols define how independently built components communicate. MCP standardizes interaction between clients and context or tool servers.
8.8.why: Core concepts should remain understandable without a specific framework.
8.8.application: Connecting a read-only tool server to an agent.
8.8.assignment: Implement a tiny workflow without a framework, then compare it with LangGraph. Inspect MCP discovery and permission boundaries using a local read-only tool.

9.1.explanation: System design chooses components and their interactions to satisfy functional needs and quality goals. Capacity estimates and trade-offs explain why a design fits a workload.
9.1.why: Architecture should follow measured requirements rather than fashionable diagrams.
9.1.application: Designing a multi-user AI request service.
9.1.assignment: Define traffic, latency and availability targets, estimate storage and concurrency, and draw a modular architecture with data flow and failure boundaries.

9.2.explanation: Caching keeps a reusable copy closer to the consumer. A hit avoids expensive work; a miss fetches from the source. Expiration and invalidation decide how stale data can become.
9.2.why: Caching trades freshness and complexity for lower latency and load.
9.2.application: Caching safe model metadata or repeated retrieval results.
9.2.assignment: Add cache-aside Redis caching with tenant-aware keys and TTL. Measure hits and misses, test invalidation and document which results must never be shared.

9.3.explanation: Rate limiting restricts how frequently a caller can act. Token buckets allow controlled bursts, while window algorithms count work over time.
9.3.why: Limits protect capacity, cost and fairness under concurrent traffic.
9.3.assignment: Implement a token bucket and a Redis-backed atomic limiter. Test simultaneous calls, expiration and 429 responses with useful retry headers.

9.4.explanation: A queue decouples a producer from a worker that performs a task later. Delivery is commonly at least once, so handlers must tolerate duplicate work.
9.4.why: Background work avoids holding an HTTP connection for long tasks.
9.4.assignment: Queue a document-processing job, make its handler idempotent, bound retries and move repeated failures to a dead-letter queue. Track status and cancellation.

9.5.explanation: Distributed systems coordinate across machines that can fail independently. Network delay and partial failure make consistency, retries and ownership difficult.
9.5.why: A request timeout does not prove that a remote operation did not happen.
9.5.application: Coordinating services and persistent request records.
9.5.assignment: Simulate a delayed response and duplicate delivery. Design idempotency keys, backoff and recovery, then explain a consistency trade-off during a network partition.

9.6.explanation: Concurrency overlaps work; parallelism executes work at the same instant. Pools and resource limits bound contention, while profiling identifies the true bottleneck.
9.6.why: More workers can reduce throughput when memory or connections are exhausted.
9.6.application: Sizing a backend's connection and worker pools.
9.6.assignment: Profile a workload, compare async I/O with a bounded thread pool and record P95 latency, throughput and memory while changing one limit at a time.

9.7.explanation: AI workloads combine variable generation time, token-dependent cost and constrained provider or GPU capacity. Routing, queues and admission control keep demand within limits.
9.7.why: Unbounded concurrency can amplify latency and cost under load.
9.7.assignment: Design a bounded inference queue, per-tenant quotas and overload behavior. Measure token throughput and first-token latency, then test graceful degradation.

9.8.explanation: Load testing applies controlled traffic to measure a system under expected and exceptional demand. Percentiles reveal slow requests that averages conceal.
9.8.why: Capacity claims need repeatable evidence and a defined environment.
9.8.application: Finding the safe request rate of your own API.
9.8.assignment: Run a small k6 test against your own service. Increase traffic gradually and report P50, P95, P99, errors, CPU and memory with the exact test conditions.

10.1.explanation: Application security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability through authentication, authorization, validation and restricted access. Threat modeling starts with what can go wrong.
10.1.why: A single missing object-level permission check can expose another user's records.
10.1.application: Securing document upload and progress endpoints.
10.1.assignment: Threat-model a small API, parameterize database queries, validate uploads and test every data route with two accounts and an anonymous caller.

10.2.explanation: LLM security treats model input and output as untrusted. Retrieved documents may contain instructions, and tools can expose data or perform unintended actions.
10.2.why: Prompt instructions alone cannot enforce an access boundary.
10.2.application: Protecting a document assistant with tool access.
10.2.assignment: Create adversarial document and prompt tests, enforce access before retrieval, validate tool arguments and require approval for sensitive actions. Record residual risks.

10.3.explanation: Tests check behavior at different boundaries: units isolate a component, integration tests connect dependencies, and end-to-end tests exercise a user journey.
10.3.why: A meaningful test detects a broken requirement instead of mirroring code.
10.3.application: Preventing regressions in a prediction API.
10.3.assignment: Write tests for valid, invalid, unauthorized and failing-provider requests. Add deterministic fixtures, a database integration test and a CI smoke journey.

10.4.explanation: AI evaluation measures quality on representative examples alongside cost and latency. Human review and automated metrics answer different questions and have different biases.
10.4.why: A model or prompt change can improve one example while degrading many others.
10.4.application: Comparing two RAG configurations before release.
10.4.assignment: Build a versioned golden dataset with expected sources and rubrics. Compare retrieval recall, faithfulness, latency and cost; inspect judge disagreement manually.

10.5.explanation: Containers package an application and its user-space dependencies into a reproducible image. Containers share the host kernel, unlike full virtual machines.
10.5.why: A repeatable runtime reduces environment-specific deployment failures.
10.5.application: Packaging an API and its supporting services.
10.5.assignment: Write a small multi-stage Dockerfile, run as a non-root user, configure health checks and use Compose for local dependencies. Keep secrets outside images.

10.6.explanation: Cloud computing rents compute, storage and managed services through APIs. Responsibility shifts depending on whether you operate virtual machines, containers or managed platforms.
10.6.why: A working cloud deployment also needs identity, backups and cost controls.
10.6.application: Deploying a small AI backend with a managed database.
10.6.assignment: Choose AWS or GCP, diagram a minimal deployment, restrict IAM, configure a budget alert and test restoration. Explore other providers only when required.

10.7.explanation: DevOps connects development and operations through automation and feedback. CI checks changes; delivery pipelines package and release them reproducibly.
10.7.why: Reliable releases need tested rollback and separate environment settings.
10.7.application: Releasing an API from a reviewed Git change.
10.7.assignment: Create a GitHub Actions pipeline for checks and image builds, protect deployment secrets and document rollback. Treat Kubernetes and advanced Terraform as later options.

10.8.explanation: Observability uses logs, metrics and traces to explain system behavior. Service-level objectives turn user expectations into measurable reliability targets.
10.8.why: You cannot diagnose slow generation or failed retrieval from a single uptime number.
10.8.application: Tracing a request across retrieval and inference.
10.8.assignment: Add structured request IDs, a latency histogram and a trace spanning retrieval and provider calls. Define an SLO, alert and incident playbook without logging secrets.

10.9.explanation: MLOps manages the model lifecycle from reproducible experiments to deployment, monitoring and retraining. Data, code and model versions must stay connected.
10.9.why: Model quality can decay even when application code has not changed.
10.9.application: Tracking and safely releasing a prediction model.
10.9.assignment: Track runs in MLflow, register a model with dataset and code versions, deploy a candidate and simulate drift. Define promotion, rollback and retraining criteria.

10.10.explanation: Responsible AI combines privacy, provenance, fairness and accountable operation. Data minimization limits collection; governance records decisions and ownership.
10.10.why: Technical usefulness does not remove privacy, licensing or fairness obligations.
10.10.application: Designing document retention and access policies.
10.10.assignment: Inventory collected data, document licenses and retention, test deletion and compare subgroup performance. Consult current official regulators for applicable legal requirements.

11.1.explanation: AI system architecture integrates identity, orchestration, models, memory, storage and operations behind explicit contracts. Each component needs an owner and a failure strategy.
11.1.why: A clear architecture makes the whole platform understandable and evolvable.
11.1.assignment: Draw CCAI's request and data flows, identify trust boundaries and failure modes, and write architecture decisions for routing, storage and observability.

11.2.explanation: A model router chooses a model based on task requirements, capability, quality, latency, cost and current availability. A policy must be evaluated against a stable baseline.
11.2.why: Selecting the cheapest model is useful only when it can satisfy the task.
11.2.application: Routing CCAI requests across compatible providers.
11.2.assignment: Create a capability registry and a rule-based router using configurable prices. Test context limits, provider outages and routing quality on a labeled task set.

11.3.explanation: Model serving exposes inference through a managed runtime. Quantization, key/value caching and batching trade memory, throughput, latency and sometimes quality.
11.3.why: An optimization should improve the workload you actually need to serve.
11.3.application: Benchmarking a small local model endpoint.
11.3.assignment: Choose one serving framework, establish a baseline and compare one precision or batching change. Record hardware, quality, memory, first-token latency and throughput.

11.4.explanation: High availability reduces the effect of failures through redundancy, health checks and tested recovery. Recovery time and recovery point objectives describe acceptable interruption and data loss.
11.4.why: An untested backup is not evidence that recovery works.
11.4.application: Keeping an AI backend useful during provider failure.
11.4.assignment: Create a failure drill: stop a provider, check failover and degrade safely. Restore a backup and record measured recovery time and data loss.

11.5.explanation: Architecture trade-offs compare alternatives against a workload and constraints. Complexity, freshness, cost, quality and availability rarely improve together without limits.
11.5.why: Good engineering makes the cost of each decision visible.
11.5.assignment: Write three architecture decisions comparing realistic alternatives with measured or estimated costs. State assumptions, consequences and conditions that would change each decision.

6.7.explanation: Prompt engineering and context design turn a vague model request into an explicit, testable contract. You choose instructions, examples, evidence and output rules, then evaluate the resulting behavior on fixed cases. These techniques change the supplied information rather than the learned model weights.
6.7.why: Reliable AI applications need clear instructions and deliberate context selection, plus independent validation and regression tests. Fluent output alone is not evidence that a task was solved.
6.7.application: Designing CCAI request templates, validating model outputs and assembling evidence for a document assistant.
6.7.assignment: Write zero-shot and few-shot versions of one task using a small code-managed template. Run both against the same normal, edge and adversarial fixtures, validate structured responses with a schema, and record quality, latency and token usage. Keep credentials and private data out of fixtures; you may use supplied sample responses instead of calling a paid model.
